Adapted top two fears: (A) 'two Australians with no German address: can we legally marry in Germany, and will it count at home?' and (B) 'paperwork across two governments from the other side of the world: Australian documents apostilled and possibly translated into German, proof of capacity to marry that Australia may not issue in German form, a registry office appointment in a country we do not live in, and getting the certificate home'. payload.search_intent: Informational, legal and procedural. Ranking content is expat and marriage-visa intent; our reader is a non-resident couple flying in, which nobody serves.
payload.angle: The sourced legal guide to getting married in Germany for two Australians who do not live there. The first screen answers 'can foreigners get married in Germany?' from German official sources (the Standesamt where the wedding would happen, the Federal Foreign Office, the German Embassy in Canberra) and the Australian Embassy in Berlin, not from expat forums. Then the template sections: the registry-office route, the proof-of-capacity question for Australians, the marry-in-Australia alternative, the Australian side nobody covers, getting the German certificate recognised at home, and the invisible work of a Germany wedding week a Wedded Advisor coordinates.
serp_gaps_to_win: Organic top 3 in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and London is an Austrian ministry page, culture pieces, Facebook, Reddit, a 2011 blog, YouTube, an expat magazine and Pinterest. No German government page ranks in the top 3. The first page to state the steps from official sources wins the trust lane.
Every ranking page assumes one partner is German or lives in Germany (marriage visa, Meldebescheinigung, family reunion). The non-resident couple flying in is unserved.
Snippets conflict (21 days in Germany first vs residence certificate vs neither). A page that resolves each from an official source, dated, is the gap.

No ranking page covers the Australian side: Australian documents, DFAT apostille, German translation, the certificate of no impediment and any court exemption, recognition under the Marriage Act 1961, passport name change.
No ranking page offers the marry-in-Australia, celebrate-in-Germany route.
Everything that ranks is for expats or US and UK readers; an AUD-aware, planning-led page for Australians is absent.

outline.h2: Getting married in Germany: can foreigners marry legally?
outline.answers: The plain answer in the first 60 words, sourced, and which route applies.
must_include: Use 'getting married in germany' in the H2 and in the first 100 words.

Direct answer for two non-resident Australians (yes, yes with conditions, or no) from an official German source (Federal Foreign Office, the registry office (Standesamt) concerned, or the German Embassy in Canberra). The writer leaves [[NEEDS: research answer]] if research has not confirmed it.

Two-route comparison table: marry legally in Germany vs marry in Australia and celebrate in Germany. Columns: who it suits, where the legal part happens, extra paperwork, what the Germany day looks like.

One comparison line: Italy (live) and Malta (draft) allow non-resident couples; France requires a residence link. Place Germany against them only as research confirms. Link the live Italy legal guide; DRAFT guides conditional.
Only a civil ceremony at the registry office creates a legal marriage (snippet; confirm). Say once here, detail in H2 7.
House line: requirements change; confirm with the registry office and for your own passports.

outline.h2: Residency and eligibility for marrying in Germany
outline.answers: Who is eligible and whether any residence or presence rule applies, exactly as the official source states it.
must_include: Residency or presence requirement as the official source states it. Snippets conflict (a 2016 page says 21 days; expat pages list a residence certificate); state the official rule only and never comment on what other sites say (Jamaica rule).
Which registry office handles a couple where neither partner lives in Germany (research: the office where the wedding will take place, or a central office such as Standesamt I in Berlin).

Proof of capacity to marry: what German law asks of foreign nationals, whether Australia issues an equivalent, and if not, whether an exemption from a Higher Regional Court (Oberlandesgericht) is needed and how long it takes (research; the single biggest timing risk).
Minimum age and prior-marriage rules from the official source only, briefly.
Same-sex couples: Germany's legal position from the official text; link /expert-advice/where-can-same-sex-couples-legally-marry-abroad once added to link-map.
No immigration advice; Smartraveller pointer for entry (Schengen, ETIAS if in force; research).

outline.h2: Prefer to marry in Australia? Marry at home, celebrate in Germany
outline.answers: The route that avoids the German registry process, and how much paperwork it removes.
must_include: Malta rule: default wording assumes Germany is open. If research finds it closed or effectively closed for two non-residents, revert to 'Can't marry legally in Germany? Marry in Australia, celebrate in Germany'.
Legal ceremony in Australia with an authorised celebrant (NOIM at least one month before; link the licence pillar, DRAFT conditional), then a symbolic ceremony in Germany with no legal effect.
Which steps it removes: German translations, the capacity-to-marry exemption, the registry appointment, the German certificate and its apostille.
Template timeline rule: NOIM about 12 months out, legal ceremony a few weeks before flying; the Germany week holds no legal step.
No judgement and no 'most couples'.

outline.answers: Which papers, who issues each, and how they are prepared for Germany.
must_include: One line above the table: the registry office sets final requirements; confirm with them.

Table: document | issued by (state or territory BDM; Australian Passport Office; Federal Circuit and Family Court for divorce orders) | apostille (research) | German translation (research: sworn translator in Germany or Australia) | validity window (research: German offices often require recent issue dates).

Certificate of no impediment: which Australian office issues it (DFAT through the Australian Embassy in Berlin, or in Australia), fee 'from AUD x' with year as DFAT states it, and whether Germany accepts it or still requires a court exemption.
Divorced or widowed partners: divorce order or death certificate, official source only.

Missions: the German Embassy in Canberra and consulates in Australia, and separately the Australian Embassy in Berlin. Vietnam rule: state each mission's procedure separately; never extend one post's fee or timing to another.

outline.answers: Apostilles, German translations and the order to do them in. Addresses fear B.
must_include: Germany and Australia are both parties to the Apostille Convention (confirm on hcch.net). Do not define apostille unless a fact in the pack defines it (Jamaica rule).
Order: Australian document, DFAT apostille, translation (research whether the translator must be sworn in Germany), lodge with the registry office.
German terms (Standesamt, Ehefaehigkeitszeugnis, Anmeldung zur Eheschliessung) only if sourced; gloss each once in plain words (Malta rule).
Name spelling consistent across passport, birth certificate and forms.

outline.answers: Lodging the notice of marriage with the registry office and a backward timeline. Template H2 'Banns and timeline', adapted because Germany uses registration with the Standesamt, not banns (research confirms; if banns apply, keep the template word).
must_include: How the notice (Anmeldung zur Eheschliessung) is lodged when neither partner lives in Germany: in person, by post or by authorised representative (research), fees in EUR with source and date, processing time, and how long the registration stays valid (research).
Court exemption from the capacity certificate, if required: processing time from the official source, and its validity window.
Backward timeline table from 12 months to wedding week, labelled as an illustration, with a parallel column for the marry-in-Australia route (Vietnam rule).
Vietnam rule: when the legal answer is uncertain, advise not to pay venue deposits until the registry office answers in writing.
Malta rule: collect the unanswered points into one short 'Questions to ask the registry office' list instead of repeating 'ask' in prose.

outline.answers: Where, who officiates, language, witnesses, and the certificate.
must_include: Who marries you (a registrar) and where (registry office or an approved outside location; research). Never place a venue in a town without a source.
Language: if either partner does not speak German, whether an interpreter is required and who supplies it (research).
Witnesses: whether any are required, from the official source. Link the witnesses spoke, DRAFT conditional.
Marriage certificate: how to order an international or multilingual extract, fee in EUR dated, and whether an apostille is needed for Australia (research).

Optional, only if venue intent matters to the writer's flow: one sentence on what to check before choosing a venue (whether the registry office can marry you there, travel time from the registry office). No named castles, no Neuschwanstein claim. Search data shows castle intent at 10 a month, so no castle H3.

outline.answers: What has legal effect and the legal order of ceremonies.
must_include: A church ceremony alone has no legal effect; civil first (research; snippet only).
